commentary.bottom_line: No study has tested whether executive sponsorship and dedicated budget, staff, and infrastructure for AI governance lead to safer or more effective AI deployment, so this recommendation rests on 21 endorsing frameworks, guidance documents, and commentaries. Two descriptive studies suggest that the resource gap exists, with a median of 0% of family medicine departmental budgets allocated to AI and 68.4% of surveyed organizations reporting a lack of AI expertise.

perspectives.view: No study compares organizations with and without executive-sponsored, funded AI governance, so certainty cannot be rated above no direct evidence. The two available studies are a survey of 109 department chairs and a qualitative study of 22 leaders. They describe the hazard and do not test the practice. Endorsements are numerous but consist of expert opinion.

In one qualitative study, 52.6% of organizations reported difficulty evaluating AI effectiveness. This suggests that many sites may lack the capacity to detect a model that underperforms before it affects patients. The study does not show that added funding or executive sponsorship closes that detection gap.

Lack of AI expertise was reported by 68.4% of organizations in a study of quality and safety leaders. Validation, monitoring, and workflow design each require trained staff. Whether sponsored budgets translate into sustained monitoring with adequate fidelity in routine workflows has not been studied.

Family medicine chairs reported a median of 0% and a mean of 2.4% of departmental budget allocated to AI. The authors note that departmental figures likely undercount institutional spending. No study reports the cost, staffing levels, or return associated with funding a governance program at scale.

The HEAAL framework states that low-resource settings will need infrastructure and technical assistance investment to adopt equity practices. Neither hazard study reports results by safety-net status or payer mix. The size of the resource gap in the settings that serve Medicaid and limited English proficiency patients therefore remains unmeasured.

commentary.research_gap: Studies are needed that compare AI safety, performance monitoring completion, and patient outcomes across organizations with differing levels of executive sponsorship and dedicated governance funding. Such studies should also report the staffing and budget levels associated with adequate validation and monitoring.
commentary.underserved_note: No study tested the practice in any population. The two hazard studies surveyed department chairs and quality leaders in the United States and Canada and did not report data on Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Evidence on whether governance resourcing reaches or benefits safety-net settings is absent, and those settings may face larger resource gaps than the ones described.
